hero.headline: Pulte Homes Targets St. Lucie County Buyers with New Development
hero.body:
Pulte Homes is focusing on St. Lucie County as it markets new housing to South Florida residents seeking more affordable options. The national homebuilder sees the county as an attractive location for buyers priced out of more expensive coastal markets.

The development strategy positions St. Lucie County as a destination for South Florida bargain hunters looking to purchase homes at lower price points than those available in traditional coastal communities. Pulte operates as one of the largest homebuilders in the United States and has identified the Treasure Coast as a growth market.

St. Lucie County has experienced steady population growth in recent years as housing costs in South Florida metropolitan areas have pushed buyers to look north. Pulte's focus on the county represents continued builder confidence in the local market. The company's strategy reflects broader regional trends as employers, families, and retirees relocate to the Treasure Coast seeking lower costs of living while maintaining access to Florida's Atlantic coast.

The severity of the collision required air transport for at least one victim, indicating serious injuries sustained in the wreck. The crash involved a passenger SUV and a commercial semi-truck on the northbound lanes of the interstate.

Earlier this week, separate incidents closed portions of I-95 in Martin County, including a multi-vehicle crash near Kanner Highway that shut down all northbound lanes. The stretch of I-95 running through Martin County has seen multiple serious traffic incidents in recent days.

Motorists traveling through Martin County on I-95 should remain alert and exercise caution, particularly in high-traffic areas where commercial vehicles and passenger cars share the road. The Florida Highway Patrol typically investigates serious crashes on the interstate to determine causes and contributing factors.

cards.headline: Community members rally to save rare deep-sea coral reef off Fort Pierce coast
cards.body:
Dozens of community members gathered at the Blake Library in Martin County to protest a federally appointed council vote that rolled back longstanding protections for the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. The reef, found hundreds of feet below the surface and home to more than 2,000 marine species, exists nowhere else on Earth and thrives in deep, dark waters unlike most coral that needs shallow sunlight to survive.

The proposals to reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling follow a Trump Executive order issued in April 2025 that directed eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate fishing industries. Scientists warn that trawling destroyed as much as 90 percent of the reef before federal protections were put in place decades ago. Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the reef, told the gathering that fish depend on the coral for habitat and food. Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, joined Gilmore in urging the public to help save the reef.

Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association and a generational shrimper, believes reopening shrimping access to the Oculina Bank is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry, which he says is teetering on the brink of extinction. Council data shows the rock shrimp industry has plummeted from over 700 trips per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010. The number of active rock shrimpers dropped from 144 in 1996 to less than 30, with just 12 active boats in 2018. Zales attributes the decline to high costs, competition from imported shrimp, and closures of previously open fishing areas.

Scientists warned that reopening the reef could irreparably damage what little remains of the coral. The Oculina Bank coral grows very slowly and has been there for a long time. Perry and Gilmore emphasized that corals are in trouble worldwide and no more should be destroyed. A federal agency is now preparing a final ruling on the reef's protections, with the outcome affecting both the marine ecosystem and the struggling local shrimping industry.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years in prison for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa from a shed behind her home in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. The case came to light in May 2025 when a victim reported experiencing partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections at the makeshift facility called Miracle Hand and Spa. The victim had been referred to the business by coworkers who had previously used Mena's services.

After the victim developed paralysis, Mena refunded the $325 payment and asked the victim to return for a vitamin injection to reverse the issues. When the paralysis continued, the victim requested to see Mena's medical license. Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that had actually expired in February 2024. She also falsely claimed to be a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

Port St. Lucie Police, along with PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax, and the Florida Department of Health, executed a search warrant at Mena's residence. Detectives discovered medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines, and injection devices for fillers and Botox.

Mena was convicted on multiple charges including three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of practicing medicine without an active license, fraud charges for obtaining property through swindles, and use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The case was reported by Emma Romano and highlights the dangers of unlicensed medical procedures being performed in residential settings.

cards.headline: Split votes close and merge county middle schools
cards.teaser: A divided school board voted to close and merge middle schools in a decision that will reshape education for families across the county.
cards.body:
School board members cast split votes to close and merge middle schools, a contentious decision that will affect students and families throughout the district. The vote came after debate among board members about enrollment trends, facility conditions, and educational programming at existing middle school campuses.

Middle school consolidation typically involves reassigning students from closed campuses to remaining facilities, which can result in larger class sizes, longer bus routes, and changes to school communities that families have been part of for years. The decision affects where sixth, seventh, and eighth grade students will attend school and how resources will be distributed across remaining middle school campuses.

School districts often consider consolidation when enrollment declines or when aging facilities require expensive repairs. The split vote indicates disagreement among board members about whether closing and merging schools serves the best interests of students and the community, particularly regarding the impact on neighborhoods and family convenience.

cards.headline: Florida property tax cut proposal heads to voters in November
cards.teaser: Florida lawmakers passed a property tax cut proposal that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years. The measure requires approval from 60 percent of voters in November.
cards.body:
Florida lawmakers on Tuesday passed a property tax cut proposal that would increase the homestead exemption from $50,000 to $250,000 over two years, with inflation adjustments beginning in 2029. The bill would still need approval from 60 percent of voters in November. The measure would also lower assessment caps on non-homesteaded properties from 10 percent to 5 percent.

Experts are divided on what the ripple effects could be if the measure passes. Real estate attorney Steve Wallace, based in Boynton Beach, raised the possibility of new fees tied to local services such as the sheriff's office and fire rescue, as counties and local governments would need to find alternative ways to derive revenue. CPA Paul Miller suggested businesses could end up carrying more of the financial burden to offset lost revenue through increased annual fees.

Municipal attorney Raul Gastesi offered a different perspective, suggesting the measure could actually push home prices higher because home buyers would have more money at their disposal. Realtor Danielle Blake was skeptical of that theory, pointing to interest rates as a more significant barrier to sales than property taxes alone. All four experts acknowledged there are significant unknowns about how counties, municipalities, and markets might respond to decreasing property tax revenue. If the ballot measure passes, lawmakers would need to return to Tallahassee to work out the specifics in a bill to implement the changes.

The anniversary provides an opportunity for residents to reflect on how the community has evolved in the years since the incident and the ongoing importance of religious tolerance and community safety.

Her legacy in Cocoa includes her work on the city council and her role as a community leader. The title 'Queen of Cocoa' reflected the respect and affection residents held for her contributions to the city over many years.

The Treasure Coast has experienced significant growth in recent years, bringing challenges related to traffic, infrastructure, environmental protection, and maintaining the character of communities like Stuart, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce, and Vero Beach. Effective planning strategies can help local governments balance economic development with preservation of natural resources like the Indian River Lagoon and the quality of life that attracts residents to the area. The expert's perspective offers lessons for local officials and residents concerned about managing future growth responsibly.

cards.headline: Twelve Make-A-Wish kids sworn in as junior deputies at St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office
cards.teaser: Sheriff Richard Del Toro honored twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation by swearing them in as junior deputies at the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office hosted a special ceremony on Wednesday where twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies by Sheriff Richard Del Toro. Del Toro called it one of the greatest days in his career as the young heroes received badges and toured the facility.

Among the newest junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder requiring a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save her life, enduring a wheelchair and significant pain during the process. Mia said her brother made her feel safe during a scary time. Another junior deputy, Tobias, was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity Deleon said he experienced complications that do not normally happen to children and even stopped breathing at one point before doctors were able to revive him and he miraculously recovered.

The junior deputies received a full law enforcement experience including demonstrations from the helicopter, SWAT team, and K-9 units. Deleon expressed gratitude for the Sheriff's Office making her son feel welcomed and important in the community. Sheriff Del Toro said the children made the department's wish come true by leaving an imprint on the deputies.

Hardware stores carry high-value tools and equipment that are frequent targets for theft rings. The Sheriff's Office has not released full details about how many arrests were made or the total value of stolen merchandise recovered during Operation Hammer Time. cards.body:

Deputies found the woman behind the wheel with the engine still running, suggesting she had lost consciousness while the vehicle was operational. The presence of a minor in the vehicle resulted in enhanced charges, as Florida law treats DUI cases more seriously when children are endangered.

Dunnellon is located in Marion County, northwest of the Treasure Coast region. This incident marks the tenth motorcyclist death in Marion County traffic incidents in 2026, highlighting ongoing road safety concerns in the area. The woman faces charges related to both the impaired driving and endangering a minor.

cards.headline: Florida legislature approves expanded homestead tax exemption to appear on ballot
cards.teaser: State lawmakers have passed legislation that will place a constitutional amendment before voters to expand the homestead property tax exemption.
cards.body:
The Florida legislature has approved placing a constitutional amendment on the ballot that would expand the homestead property tax exemption available to Florida homeowners. The measure will go before voters statewide, giving residents in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties the opportunity to decide whether to increase the tax break for primary residences.

The homestead exemption reduces the taxable value of a primary residence, lowering annual property tax bills for qualifying homeowners. Expanding the exemption would mean lower tax payments for homeowners across the Treasure Coast, but would also reduce revenue available to county governments, school districts, and municipalities that rely on property taxes to fund services. Local governments in Stuart, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce, Vero Beach, and other communities depend on property tax revenue for essential services including schools, public safety, infrastructure, and parks.

Voters will decide whether the tax savings for individual homeowners outweigh the potential impact on local government budgets and services. If approved, the expanded exemption would apply to homesteaded properties throughout Florida, including thousands of homes across the three-county Treasure Coast region.

cards.headline: Florida property tax changes could affect children's services funding
cards.teaser: Proposed property tax reforms in Florida may reduce revenue streams that support programs and services for children across the state.
cards.body:
Changes to Florida's property tax structure could reduce funding for programs that serve children throughout the state, including communities across the Treasure Coast. Property tax revenue supports school district operations, after-school programs, child welfare services, and recreation facilities that families in Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties rely on for their children.

Local governments and school districts in Stuart, Port St. Lucie, Fort Pierce, Vero Beach, and surrounding areas depend heavily on property tax collections to maintain services for young residents. Reductions in property tax revenue can lead to cuts in school staffing, elimination of programs, reduced library hours, and fewer recreational opportunities for children and families.

Advocates for children's services argue that property tax reforms should account for the impact on programs that serve young people, ensuring that tax relief for homeowners does not come at the expense of educational quality, safety, and developmental opportunities for children growing up in Florida communities.

Top high school baseball players from Southwest Florida have earned recognition on the all-area team, celebrating the region's best talent from the recently completed season. The selections honor student athletes who excelled on the diamond at schools across the area, including programs that compete against Treasure Coast teams in regional playoffs and tournaments.

cards.headline: Martin County schools police chief arrested for DUI

The police chief for Martin County schools was arrested on DUI charges, according to law enforcement reports. The arrest raises questions about leadership within the district's police department, which is responsible for safety across all Martin County public schools.

The Martin County School District Police Department oversees security at schools throughout the county, including facilities in Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, Hobe Sound, and Indiantown. The arrest comes at a time when school safety remains a priority for Martin County families. Parents and staff rely on the school district police force to maintain secure learning environments and respond to incidents on campuses throughout the county.

hero.headline: Threshers Sweep St. Lucie Mets in Doubleheader at Clover Park
hero.body:
The Clearwater Threshers swept the St. Lucie Mets in a doubleheader at Clover Park on Wednesday, handing the local minor league team a double defeat. The games were played after Tuesday's scheduled matchup between the two teams was postponed.

The six-game series at Clover Park in Port St. Lucie had been set to run through the week, but weather or scheduling issues forced the Tuesday postponement. The Mets and Threshers made up the lost game by playing two on Wednesday.

The Threshers took both contests, dealing the Mets losses in front of their home fans at the Port St. Lucie ballpark. Clover Park serves as both the spring training home of the New York Mets and the regular season home of the St. Lucie Mets, who compete in the Florida State League.

The series between the Mets and Threshers continues as part of the minor league baseball season. Fans who attend games at Clover Park can watch prospects from the New York Mets organization compete against other teams in the league throughout the summer.

The matchup against the Threshers, an affiliate of the Philadelphia Phillies, is part of the Florida State League schedule. Local fans can attend games throughout the series to support the home team and enjoy affordable family entertainment at one of the area's premier baseball facilities.

The weekend celebration emphasizes the importance of youth sports and active lifestyles in communities throughout the region.

Coconut Creek High School in Broward County is earning respect for its football program as the summer begins, with several quality prospects continuing to make strides in their development. The school has become a destination for talent evaluation and exposure.

The Florida High School Athletic Association has released the playoff format for its Open Division, introducing a new structure for the state's elite high school football programs. The format is designed to pit the top teams against each other in postseason competition.

hero.headline: Beetlejuice musical runs through June 7 at West Palm Beach Kravis Center
hero.body:
The Broadway hit Beetlejuice the musical is playing at the Kravis Center through June 7, bringing Tim Burton's spooky comedy to the Alexander W. Dreyfoos Concert Hall. Actor Ryan Stajmiger stars as the mischievous demon in the iconic striped suit, a role he has loved since childhood. The musical follows Lydia Deetz, a strange and unusual teen whose life changes after meeting two recently deceased neighbors and a demon with a flair for trouble.

Stajmiger says one of his favorite parts of the show is breaking the fourth wall and communicating directly with the audience. He experienced an unexpected moment early in the run when a wig change went wrong on stage. He was wearing two wigs, and the second wig came off with the first, leaving him bald for an entire scene. He got to play with that moment and share the surprise with the audience.

Performances include 7:30 p.m. shows on June 3 and June 4, 8 p.m. on June 5, matinee and evening performances on June 6, and a closing matinee on June 7. Tickets start at $34.50 and are available at kravis.org. The show is recommended for ages 13 and up, with parental discretion advised.

The Kravis Center continues to draw major Broadway productions, offering Palm Beach County residents access to big-stage experiences and boosting the region as a cultural destination. The West Palm Beach venue has become a key stop for touring shows bringing professional theater to South Florida audiences.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach hosts finish line for 80-mile cystic fibrosis paddle from Bahamas June 13
cards.teaser: More than 100 paddlers will cross 80 miles of open Atlantic Ocean from Bimini to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to raise funds for families living with cystic fibrosis.
cards.body:
The annual Crossing for Cystic Fibrosis will bring more than 100 paddlers to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 after a 12 to 16 hour endurance paddle from Bimini, Bahamas. According to event founder Travis Suit, participants will launch from Bimini at midnight on June 13 and arrive at Lake Worth Beach for a daylong beach celebration. The event benefits the Pipers Angels Foundation, which Suit established in honor of his daughter, Piper, who was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis at age 4.

The crossing is part of a four-day schedule beginning June 10 with arrivals and a poolside social at Bimini Cove. On Thursday, participants take part in a 4Ocean beach cleanup and a community buffet dinner. Friday brings a Paddle Out Rose Ceremony to honor cystic fibrosis warriors, followed by rest and safety checks before the midnight launch. All paddlers are required to wear a U.S. Coast Guard approved personal flotation device, waterproof whistle, and reflective gear during dark hours. GPS trackers provided by the event must be worn and active at all times, and mandatory safety meetings will be held.

Paddlers must raise at least $2,000 for the cause, while crew or virtual participants have a $500 minimum. Final contributions are due July 31. Suit, an avid paddler, was inspired to create the event after learning about the natural respiratory benefits of ocean salt air. The foundation has grown to provide direct support for cystic fibrosis patients and families, connecting them with resources and community. Spectators are invited to Lake Worth Beach on June 13 to cheer paddlers during the arrival celebration. More information is available at crossingforcysticfibrosis.com and pipersangels.org.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast celebrates America's 250th Fourth of July with events across region
cards.teaser: The Treasure Coast will mark America's 250th birthday this Fourth of July with celebrations across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.
cards.body:
The Treasure Coast is preparing for Fourth of July festivities to mark America's 250th birthday, with events planned across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties. The milestone anniversary will bring communities together for parades, fireworks, and celebrations throughout the region.

The Fourth of July falls on a Friday this year, creating a long weekend for celebrations. Communities across the Treasure Coast typically host patriotic events including parades, concerts, and fireworks displays. The 250th anniversary of American independence is expected to draw larger crowds and more elaborate celebrations than typical years.

Residents can expect traditional Independence Day activities including family gatherings, beach visits, and evening fireworks shows. Local officials encourage families to participate in community events and celebrate the historic milestone together. The Treasure Coast's coastal location makes it a popular destination for Fourth of July weekend, with beaches and waterfront parks serving as gathering spots for residents and visitors.

cards.headline: Florida fireworks laws remain in effect for Fourth of July celebrations
cards.teaser: Florida residents should be aware of state fireworks laws as Fourth of July celebrations approach for America's 250th birthday.
cards.body:
Florida's fireworks regulations will be in effect during the Fourth of July holiday weekend as communities across the state prepare to celebrate America's 250th birthday. The laws govern what types of fireworks can be used and when they can be set off by private citizens.

Florida law distinguishes between sparklers and other novelty items that are legal year round, and larger fireworks that are typically restricted to certain holidays. Many counties and municipalities also have local ordinances that may be more restrictive than state law. Residents planning to use fireworks should check both state regulations and local rules in their communities.

The Fourth of July is one of the holidays when Florida law allows expanded use of certain fireworks. However, safety remains a priority, and authorities encourage residents to attend professional fireworks displays rather than setting off fireworks at home. Fire departments across the Treasure Coast typically see an increase in calls related to fireworks during the holiday weekend.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast walkability varies by community, EPA data shows
cards.teaser: Communities across the Treasure Coast show different levels of walkability, according to Environmental Protection Agency data that ranks areas based on pedestrian access.
cards.body:
The Environmental Protection Agency has released walkability data for communities across the Treasure Coast, showing how easily residents can access destinations on foot. The rankings measure factors like street connectivity, proximity to services, and pedestrian infrastructure in cities and neighborhoods across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties.

Walkability affects quality of life, property values, and community health. Areas with higher walkability scores typically have better connected street networks, more mixed-use development, and destinations like shops, restaurants, and services within walking distance. Downtown areas in cities like Stuart, Fort Pierce, and Vero Beach generally score higher than suburban neighborhoods designed primarily for car travel.

The data can help residents and prospective homebuyers understand how easily they can walk to daily destinations in different Treasure Coast communities. It also provides local governments with information to guide planning decisions about sidewalks, crosswalks, and development patterns that support pedestrian activity.

cards.headline: Five public golf courses on Treasure Coast offer range of prices and skill levels
cards.teaser: Golfers on the Treasure Coast can choose from public courses offering a range of prices and challenges to suit different budgets and abilities.
cards.body:
The Treasure Coast offers five public golf courses with varying price points and difficulty levels, giving local golfers options to match their budget and skill level. The courses across Martin, St. Lucie, and Indian River counties provide access to the sport for residents and visitors without requiring country club memberships.

Public golf courses serve an important role in communities by making the sport accessible to a broader range of players. The Treasure Coast's mild climate allows for year-round golf, making the region attractive to both serious golfers and casual players. Course conditions, amenities, and green fees vary across the public facilities.

Local golfers can research rates and course layouts to find the best fit for their game and budget. Many public courses offer twilight rates, senior discounts, and package deals that make golf more affordable. The variety of options helps support the Treasure Coast's reputation as a golf-friendly region.

cards.headline: Indian River County grapefruit featured in Jeopardy question
cards.teaser: Indian River County's famous grapefruit was the subject of a $2,000 question on the game show Jeopardy, highlighting the region's citrus heritage.
cards.body:
Indian River County earned national recognition when its grapefruit appeared as a $2,000 question on Jeopardy. The game show reference highlighted the county's reputation for producing some of Florida's finest citrus. Indian River County grapefruit has long been prized for its sweetness and quality, supported by the region's ideal growing conditions.

The citrus industry has been a cornerstone of the Treasure Coast economy for generations. Indian River County's location along Florida's east coast provides the right combination of climate, soil, and water to produce premium grapefruit. The Indian River name carries weight in citrus markets and is protected as a regional designation.

The Jeopardy appearance brings positive attention to the local agriculture industry at a time when Florida citrus faces challenges from disease and development pressure. Indian River County's citrus heritage remains an important part of the region's identity and economy, even as groves face ongoing threats from greening disease and urban growth.

hero.headline: Florida Highway Patrol Arrests Man for Stealing and Attempting to Sell Radioactive Device in Manatee County
hero.body:
The Florida Highway Patrol arrested a man in Manatee County for theft and possession of a radiological device after he allegedly attempted to sell the stolen radioactive equipment on Facebook. The arrest highlights concerns about public safety and the security of sensitive materials across Florida.

According to law enforcement, the suspect was apprehended by Florida Highway Patrol after attempting to market the radioactive device through the social media platform. The incident raises questions about how such dangerous materials can be stolen and the potential risks posed to communities when radiological equipment falls into unauthorized hands. Radioactive devices are typically used in industrial, medical, or scientific applications and require strict handling protocols due to their potential health hazards.

The arrest in Manatee County underscores the ongoing challenges Florida law enforcement faces in tracking and securing hazardous materials. Radiological devices can pose significant public health risks if mishandled or improperly stored. The Florida Highway Patrol's involvement in this case demonstrates the coordination between state agencies in responding to threats involving dangerous materials that could affect public safety across multiple jurisdictions.

The investigation into how the device was stolen and whether additional suspects are involved continues. Possession of radiological materials without proper authorization violates both state and federal regulations designed to protect the public from radiation exposure. The case serves as a reminder to Florida businesses and institutions that use such equipment to maintain robust security measures. Florida Highway Patrol has not released the suspect's name or the specific type of radiological device involved, but the arrest marks a significant interception of potentially dangerous material before it could change hands through an illicit sale.

cards.headline: Florida Education Commissioner Kamoutsas Named President of Polk State College
cards.teaser: Florida's education commissioner has been appointed to lead Polk State College, marking a significant leadership transition in the state's higher education system.
cards.body:
Florida Education Commissioner Kamoutsas has been named the new president of Polk State College, according to announcements from the institution. The appointment represents a major administrative change for the college and for the state's education leadership.

The transition brings extensive state-level education experience to the college presidency. As education commissioner, Kamoutsas oversaw policy and operations affecting Florida's entire public education system, including K-12 schools and state colleges. The move from a statewide administrative role to a college presidency is a notable shift that will affect both the Department of Education and Polk State College as they navigate leadership transitions.

Polk State College serves students in Central Florida, and the new leadership appointment comes at a time when Florida's higher education institutions face ongoing discussions about funding, enrollment, and academic priorities. The college will benefit from Kamoutsas's experience in state education policy, while the Department of Education will need to fill the commissioner position to continue overseeing Florida's educational programs statewide.

cards.headline: Florida CFO Urges Voters to Reject Government Claims on Property Tax
cards.teaser: The state's chief financial officer is advising Florida voters to disregard what he calls hype from big government supporters regarding property tax policies.
cards.body:
Florida's Chief Financial Officer is calling on voters across the state to ignore messaging from what he characterizes as big government apologists concerning property tax issues. The statement from the CFO represents a significant political positioning on tax policy ahead of potential ballot measures or legislative debates.

Property taxes remain a central concern for Florida homeowners, particularly as property values and insurance costs have increased in recent years. The CFO's public statement suggests ongoing political disagreement about how property tax policy should be structured and what information voters receive about proposed changes. Florida's property tax system includes homestead exemptions and Save Our Homes protections that limit assessment increases for primary residences.

The CFO's comments indicate that property tax policy will likely be a significant issue in upcoming political discussions. As a statewide elected official responsible for managing state finances, the CFO's position carries weight in debates about taxation and government spending. Florida voters will need to navigate competing claims about property tax proposals as they consider how these policies affect homeowners, local government funding, and public services across the state.

cards.headline: Florida DOT Plans Improvements for Major Orlando-Area Interchange
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Transportation is developing plans to address traffic issues at a critical junction connecting SR-528, Florida's Turnpike, and Orange Blossom Trail.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation has announced plans to fix the interchange connecting State Road 528, Florida's Turnpike, and Orange Blossom Trail in the Orlando area. The planned improvements target one of Central Florida's busiest traffic junctions, which serves both local commuters and tourists traveling to and from Orlando International Airport and theme parks.

The interchange handles significant daily traffic volume as it connects major transportation corridors in the region. SR-528, also known as the Beachline Expressway, provides a direct route between Orlando and the Space Coast. Florida's Turnpike is a major north-south toll road serving the entire state. Orange Blossom Trail is a key arterial road through the Orlando metropolitan area. The convergence of these routes creates complex traffic patterns that the FDOT improvements aim to address.

Transportation infrastructure projects in Florida's growing metropolitan areas are essential to managing congestion and supporting economic activity. The Orlando region continues to experience population growth and tourism demand, putting pressure on existing road networks. FDOT's planning process will determine the scope and timeline for the interchange improvements, which will affect commuters, commercial traffic, and visitors traveling through Central Florida.

Investigators are working to establish the full details of what occurred and how the stabbing and death are related. The incident serves as a reminder of the importance of campus safety measures and community awareness. Florida's universities work closely with local law enforcement to maintain security and respond to incidents that affect student and community safety across their campuses and surrounding neighborhoods.

cards.headline: Florida A&M and Florida State Researchers Develop AI System to Connect Cars and Traffic Signals

cards.body:
Researchers at the joint College of Engineering operated by Florida A&M University and Florida State University are developing technology to make streets smarter through artificial intelligence. The smart street initiative represents the type of advanced transportation research taking place at Florida's public universities. The collaboration between FAMU and FSU leverages the strengths of both institutions in engineering and technology development.

As Florida's cities grow and traffic volumes increase, innovative solutions to transportation challenges become increasingly important. The research could have applications throughout the state and beyond, positioning Florida universities as leaders in intelligent transportation systems. The development of such technology also aligns with broader trends toward connected and autonomous vehicles that will shape the future of transportation across Florida and the nation.

The teacher shortage affects school districts across Florida, impacting class sizes, course offerings, and educational quality. State initiatives like the Grow Your Own Teacher Grant aim to create sustainable solutions by building a pipeline of new educators. The investment in teacher development is part of broader efforts to strengthen Florida's education system and ensure that schools can attract and retain the teaching talent needed to serve the state's growing student population.

hero.headline: One person airlifted with traumatic injuries after SUV-semi truck collision on I-95 in Martin County
hero.body:
First responders airlifted one person with traumatic injuries following a collision between an SUV and a semi-truck on Interstate 95 in Martin County. The crash occurred Thursday morning and prompted a significant emergency response.

The severity of the collision required air transport for at least one victim, indicating serious injuries sustained in the wreck. The crash involved a passenger SUV and a commercial semi-truck on the northbound lanes of the interstate.

Earlier this week, separate incidents closed portions of I-95 in Martin County, including a multi-vehicle crash near Kanner Highway that shut down all northbound lanes. The stretch of I-95 running through Martin County has seen multiple serious traffic incidents in recent days.

Motorists traveling through Martin County on I-95 should remain alert and exercise caution, particularly in high-traffic areas where commercial vehicles and passenger cars share the road. The Florida Highway Patrol typically investigates serious crashes on the interstate to determine causes and contributing factors.

cards.headline: All northbound lanes of I-95 closed near Kanner Highway in Martin County after multi-vehicle crash
cards.teaser: A multi-vehicle crash shut down all northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Kanner Highway in Martin County, causing significant traffic disruptions.
cards.body:
All northbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Kanner Highway in Martin County were closed following a multi-vehicle crash. The closure affected a major traffic corridor through the county, forcing motorists to seek alternate routes or face extended delays.

The crash near Kanner Highway represents one of several serious traffic incidents on I-95 in Martin County this week. The highway serves as a primary north-south route through the Treasure Coast, and full closures create ripple effects throughout the region's road network.

Kanner Highway intersects I-95 in the Stuart area, a busy commercial and residential corridor. When major crashes close all lanes of the interstate, local roads including Kanner Highway, Monterey Road, and other east-west routes typically experience increased congestion as drivers seek alternative paths. First responders work to clear serious crashes as quickly as possible while ensuring thorough investigation and safe conditions for reopening.

cards.headline: Martin County residents rally at Blake Library to save Oculina Bank coral reef off Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: Dozens of community members gathered at Blake Library in Martin County after a federal council voted to roll back protections for a rare deep-water coral reef found nowhere else on Earth.
cards.body:
Dozens of Martin County residents gathered at Blake Library to advocate for protecting the Oculina Bank, a rare deep-water coral reef located just off the coast of Fort Pierce. The community meeting followed a vote by a federally appointed council to roll back longstanding protections for the reef, which exists hundreds of feet below the surface and is home to more than 2,000 marine species.

Dr. Grant Gilmore, a scientist who previously dived the rare reef, told attendees he is concerned about the ecosystem. "Your fish don't exist in a vacuum, they need a habitat, they need food," Gilmore said. "The coral reef was giving them habitat and food. You take that away, you don't have the fish." Mark Perry, Executive Director of the Florida Oceanographic Society, joined Gilmore in urging the public to help save the reef, noting that corals grow very slowly and have been in place for a long time.

Two proposals would reopen parts of the reef to shrimp trawling, even though scientists say trawling destroyed as much as 90% of the reef before federal protections were established decades ago. The proposals followed a Trump executive order issued in April 2025 that directed eight regional councils nationwide to find ways to reinvigorate fishing industries. Bob Zales, executive director of the Southeastern Fishing Association, has argued that reopening shrimping access is essential for the struggling rock shrimp industry, which has seen trips plummet from over 700 per year in the mid-1990s to under 100 since 2010.

cards.headline: Wire 3 announces $53 million investment to power three Martin County communities
cards.teaser: Wire 3 is making a $53 million investment to bring power infrastructure to three communities in Martin County.
cards.body:
Wire 3 announced a $53 million investment aimed at powering up three communities in Martin County. The substantial infrastructure investment will enhance electrical service and capacity for residents and businesses in the affected areas.

The project represents a significant commitment to Martin County's infrastructure development and power grid reliability. Large-scale electrical infrastructure investments typically involve upgrading transmission lines, substations, and distribution networks to meet growing demand and improve service quality.

Martin County has experienced steady growth in recent years, particularly in areas like Palm City, Jensen Beach, and other unincorporated communities. Infrastructure investments of this scale often support both existing residents and anticipated future development, ensuring adequate power supply for homes, businesses, and public facilities across the county.

cards.headline: Martin County beach project receives national restoration award
cards.teaser: A beach restoration project in Martin County has been recognized with a national award for its environmental and coastal preservation work.
cards.body:
A Martin County beach has earned a national restoration award, recognizing the successful work to preserve and restore the coastal environment. The award highlights the county's commitment to protecting its shoreline and natural resources along the Atlantic coast.

Martin County's beaches face ongoing challenges from erosion, storm damage, and rising sea levels. Beach restoration projects typically involve sand replenishment, dune stabilization, and habitat protection measures that benefit both wildlife and public beach access. The recognition comes from a national organization that evaluates coastal restoration efforts across the country.

The county's beaches, including those in Jensen Beach, Hutchinson Island, and other coastal areas, attract both residents and tourists while providing critical habitat for sea turtles and shorebirds. Successful restoration projects balance environmental protection with recreational access, ensuring beaches remain healthy and accessible for future generations.

cards.headline: Florida city considers allowing backyard chickens under new proposal
cards.teaser: A Florida city is weighing a proposal that would allow residents to keep chickens in their backyards under certain conditions.
cards.body:
A Florida city is considering whether to allow residents to keep chickens in their backyards, a proposal that would change current zoning and animal regulations. The potential policy shift reflects growing interest in urban agriculture and self-sufficiency among homeowners.

Backyard chicken ordinances typically include restrictions on the number of birds allowed, coop placement and construction requirements, and prohibitions on roosters to minimize noise complaints. Many cities across Florida have adopted similar regulations in recent years as residents seek to raise their own eggs and embrace sustainable living practices.

Proponents of backyard chickens cite benefits including fresh eggs, natural pest control, and educational opportunities for children. Opponents often raise concerns about noise, odors, predators, and property values. City officials must balance these competing interests while crafting regulations that protect both chicken keepers and their neighbors.

cards.headline: Heiress purchasing 8 acres in Florida to preserve land from development
cards.teaser: An heiress is buying 8 acres of Florida land with plans to preserve it from future development.
cards.body:
An heiress is purchasing 8 acres of land in Florida with the intention of protecting it from development. The acquisition represents a private conservation effort aimed at preserving natural areas in the face of ongoing development pressure across the state.

Florida has experienced rapid population growth and development in recent decades, leading to loss of natural habitats, wetlands, and green spaces. Private land conservation efforts complement public preservation programs, with landowners and conservation buyers working to protect environmentally sensitive or historically significant properties.

The 8-acre parcel will remain undeveloped under the heiress's ownership, ensuring the land retains its natural character. Such conservation purchases often protect wildlife habitat, water resources, and scenic views while preventing the conversion of natural areas to residential or commercial use. Florida's remaining undeveloped lands face increasing pressure as the state's population continues to grow.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff swears in 12 Make-A-Wish children as junior deputies
hero.teaser: Twelve children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation were sworn in as junior deputies at the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, experiencing demonstrations from SWAT, K-9 units and the helicopter team.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office honored 12 children from the Make-A-Wish Foundation on Wednesday by swearing them in as junior deputies. Sheriff Richard Del Toro led the ceremony, calling it one of the greatest days in his career. The young heroes received badges, toured the sheriff's office and witnessed demonstrations from the SWAT team, K-9 unit and helicopter crew.

Among the newest junior deputies were twins Mia and Daryl Nyack. In 2023, Mia was diagnosed with aplastic anemia, a blood disorder requiring a bone marrow transplant. Her twin brother Daryl donated his bone marrow to save her life, enduring significant pain and spending time in a wheelchair during the process. Mia said her brother made her feel safe during the frightening experience. Another junior deputy honored was Tobias Deleon, who was diagnosed with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia in 2022. His mother Charity said he experienced severe complications and was even clinically deceased at one point before doctors were able to bring him back and he miraculously recovered.

The families expressed gratitude for the special day. Charity Deleon thanked the sheriff's office for making the time and energy to welcome the children into the community and remind them that they are important. Sheriff Del Toro said the children left an imprint on his department, telling them they made his wish come true.

cards.body:

The funeral will give colleagues, friends and community members a chance to celebrate Whitehead's dedication to protecting St. Lucie County residents. Firefighters and emergency personnel from across the region are expected to attend the service to show their support and solidarity.

The conversion of the empty building into an educational facility brings new life to the downtown district while addressing educational needs in the community. The project represents an investment in both education and urban renewal for Fort Pierce.

The new school is expected to serve students in the area and contribute to the ongoing efforts to strengthen downtown Fort Pierce as a hub of activity. The reuse of the vacant building also helps address concerns about empty storefronts and underutilized real estate in the city center.

cards.headline: Black bear spotted in Tradition's Town Park community
cards.teaser: Residents of the Town Park community in Tradition reported seeing a black bear in the neighborhood this week.
cards.body:
A black bear was spotted in the Town Park community in Tradition, prompting residents to take extra caution. The sighting is a reminder that wildlife encounters can occur in residential areas, particularly in communities near natural habitats.

Black bears are native to Florida and occasionally wander into neighborhoods in search of food or as they move between territories. Wildlife officials typically advise residents to secure garbage, remove bird feeders and avoid leaving pet food outside to prevent attracting bears.

The Town Park community is part of the larger Tradition development in Port St. Lucie. Residents who encounter bears should keep their distance, make noise to encourage the animal to leave and report sightings to the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. Bears usually move on quickly if they do not find food sources.

cards.headline: Lightning strike likely caused house fire, closed Florida road
cards.teaser: A house fire believed to be caused by a lightning strike forced the closure of a local road as firefighters responded to the scene.
cards.body:
A house fire likely sparked by a lightning strike required road closures as emergency crews worked to contain the blaze. The incident serves as a reminder of the dangers posed by severe weather, particularly during Florida's thunderstorm season.

Firefighters responded to the scene and worked to extinguish the fire while the affected road remained closed to allow emergency vehicles access and ensure public safety. Lightning strikes can cause immediate fires or smolder for hours before igniting, making them particularly dangerous.

Homeowners are encouraged to ensure their properties have proper lightning protection systems and to inspect for damage after severe storms. The road closure allowed first responders to work safely and prevented traffic from interfering with firefighting operations.

cards.headline: Affidavit reveals new details in second St. Lucie County school bus driver molestation case

An affidavit has revealed additional details in a second molestation case involving a St. Lucie County school bus driver. The case adds to concerns about child safety on school transportation and the screening processes for drivers who work with students.

The affidavit provides insight into the allegations and the investigation being conducted by law enforcement. Cases involving school personnel and children are treated with high priority by investigators and school district officials.

The St. Lucie County school district works closely with law enforcement when allegations arise involving staff members. Parents and guardians are encouraged to talk with their children about reporting any uncomfortable situations or inappropriate behavior by adults in positions of authority.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie woman sentenced to 3 years for running illegal med spa out of backyard shed
cards.teaser: Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St.
cards.body:
Rosa Mena, 50, of Port St. Lucie has been sentenced to three years in prison and five years of probation after operating an unlicensed medical spa out of a shed behind her home on Northwest Coosa Drive. Mena ran a business called Miracle Hand and Spa from the backyard structure, where she performed Botox injections and other cosmetic procedures without proper medical licensing.

The case came to light in May 2025 when a victim reported to police that she experienced partial facial paralysis after receiving 62 units of Botox injections from Mena. The victim, who was referred to the business by coworkers who had previously used Mena's services, paid $325 for the treatment. When the victim confronted Mena about the paralysis, Mena refunded the money but asked the victim to return for another injection of vitamins to reverse the problems. When the victim requested to see Mena's medical license, Mena provided an altered phlebotomy certificate that had actually expired in February 2024. Mena also told the victim she was a doctor from the Dominican Republic.

A multi-agency investigation involving Port St. Lucie Police, PSL Code Enforcement, the PSL Building Department, PSL Business Tax and the Florida Department of Health led to a search warrant at Mena's residence in the 5000 block of Northwest Coosa Drive. Detectives found medical beds, fat sculpting machines, laser hair removal equipment, laser liposuction machines and injection devices for fillers and Botox inside the shed.

Mena was charged with three counts of aggravated battery causing bodily harm, three counts of health safety practicing medicine without an active license, one count of fraud obtaining property worth $300 or more, one count of fraud obtaining property under $20,000 and one count of use of a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony. The sentence was handed down this week, bringing closure to a case that highlighted the dangers of unlicensed medical practices.

hero.headline: Indian River Mall Demolition Underway in Vero Beach
hero.body:

The demolition represents a significant change to the local commercial landscape in Indian River County. The mall had served the Vero Beach community for years as a central shopping destination before declining foot traffic and changing retail patterns led to its closure.

According to reports, the project has found support across different groups in the community. One source described the demolition as something that "satisfies everyone," suggesting broad agreement that redevelopment of the site represents the best path forward for the property.

The demolition work continues as the community looks ahead to what will replace the mall. The site on Indian River Boulevard represents a significant piece of real estate in Vero Beach, and its future development will likely shape the area for years to come.

The project reflects ongoing efforts by community groups in Indian River County to support families facing housing challenges. Local nonprofits have been working to connect families with resources and opportunities for stable, affordable housing across the Treasure Coast.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Pioneer to Receive Florida Historical Marker

A historical marker will be installed in Vero Beach honoring one of the city's pioneers. The Florida historical marker will recognize the individual's role in the early development and history of the community.

The marker program is managed by the state to commemorate significant people, places, and events in Florida history. Vero Beach has a rich pioneer history dating back to the early 20th century, when the area was first developed and began to grow into the community it is today.

The installation of the marker will provide residents and visitors with information about the pioneer's contributions to Vero Beach. Historical markers serve as educational tools and reminders of the individuals who shaped local communities across Florida.

cards.headline: World War II Veteran Bill Keegan Celebrates 102nd Birthday in Indian River County
cards.teaser: Bill Keegan, a World War II veteran living in Indian River County, celebrated his 102nd birthday this week.
cards.body:
Bill Keegan, a World War II veteran residing in Indian River County, marked his 102nd birthday this week. The milestone celebration honored a man who served his country during the war and has now lived more than a century.

Keegan is among the dwindling number of World War II veterans still living. The men and women who served during the 1940s conflict are now in their late 90s and beyond, making each birthday an occasion to remember their service and sacrifice.

Indian River County is home to a community of veterans from various conflicts. The area's veteran population includes survivors of World War II, Korea, Vietnam, and more recent conflicts, with local organizations and residents making efforts to honor their service.

The school districts serving St. Lucie, Martin, and Indian River counties have released their summer vacation dates for the year. The schedules outline when students will be out of school for the summer break and when classes will resume in the fall.

Summer vacation dates vary slightly between the three districts based on their individual academic calendars. Parents and students across the Treasure Coast can now plan for the break, which typically runs from late spring through mid-August before the new school year begins.

The three county school districts serve thousands of students across the region. Information about specific start and end dates for each district is available through the individual school system websites and offices.
